chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isma'il ibn Jabir

And a breeze occurred to him in his face due to an ailment that afflicted him while he was in ihram. He said, so I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'The doctor who treats me prescribed for me sa'uut (nasal drops) containing musk.' He said, 'Use it.' As for the perfume that must be avoided, there are four things: musk, ambergris, saffron, and waras. And it has been narrated [also] al-ud (agarwood).

key_terms.إِحْرَامٌ: The state of consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.اَلْوَرْسُ: Waras (a type of tree resin/wood used for scent)
key_terms.سَعُوطٌ: Nasal drops or snuff used for medicinal purposes

ai.seo_question: What perfumes are forbidden for a pilgrim in ihram, and is musk allowed for medicine?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between general prohibition of scent and specific medicinal necessity, citing Imam al-Sadiq’s permission to use musk-based snuff for treating a wind-related ailment. It highlights the scholarly consensus on the four primary prohibited scents—musk, ambergris, saffron, and waras—while noting the variant inclusion of agarwood, reflecting the nuanced juristic approach to *ihram* restrictions in Shia fiqh.
